8.0.big: Almost all the energy in the food you eat started out as sunlight captured by photosynthesis.
points: Photosynthetic organisms (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) are the base of almost every food web.
When the wrong algae overgrow (an algal bloom), they can wipe out sea grass and everything that depends on it.

8.1.big: Photosynthesis uses light energy to turn CO2 and water into sugar, giving off oxygen. It happens in the chloroplast.
points: Photoautotrophs (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) make their own food from light. Heterotrophs (animals, fungi, most bacteria) eat others. Chemoautotrophs get energy from inorganic chemicals instead of light.
Overall: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O + light → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. That's cellular respiration run backwards.
Leaves take in CO2 through stomata (pores mostly on the underside). Photosynthesis happens in the mesophyll cells.
Inside the chloroplast: stacks of thylakoids (each stack is a granum) hold the chlorophyll. The fluid around them is the stroma.
Two stages: the light-dependent reactions (in the thylakoid membranes) make ATP and NADPH, then the Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses them to build sugar.
8.1.tip: Stoma = mouth (a pore in the leaf). Stroma = the fluid inside the chloroplast. One letter apart, totally different places.

8.2.big: The light-dependent reactions catch sunlight with pigments and use it to split water, giving off O2, and to make the energy carriers ATP and NADPH.
points: Shorter wavelength means more energy. Violet and blue carry more than red. UV and X-rays carry so much they damage cells.
Chlorophyll a and b absorb blue and red light and reflect green, which is why plants look green. Carotenoids absorb blue-green and safely get rid of extra energy as heat.
Photosystem II goes first: light excites electrons, and the electrons it loses are replaced by splitting water. That's where the O2 comes from.
Electrons travel down an electron transport chain (with the cytochrome complex) to photosystem I, pumping H+ into the thylakoid space on the way.
Photosystem I re-energizes the electrons with more light and hands them to NADP+, making NADPH.
H+ rushes back out through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. That's chemiosmosis again, just like in mitochondria.
8.2.tip: Photosystem II comes before photosystem I in the chain. They're numbered by when they were discovered, not by order.

8.3.big: The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix CO2 from the air into sugar.
points: 1. Fixation: the enzyme RuBisCO attaches CO2 to RuBP (5 carbons), making two 3-PGA molecules. This is carbon fixation: inorganic carbon becomes organic.
2. Reduction: ATP and NADPH turn 3-PGA into G3P, a 3-carbon sugar.
3. Regeneration: most G3P is recycled (with more ATP) to rebuild RuBP so the cycle keeps going.
It takes 3 turns (3 CO2) to make one extra G3P that can leave the cycle, and two G3P can build a glucose.
Desert plants like cacti open their stomata at night to save water (CAM photosynthesis).
Photosynthesis and respiration are a loop: one makes the O<sub>2</sub> and sugar the other uses, and the other makes the CO<sub>2</sub> and water the first one needs.

1.why: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, so they have no chloroplasts. They do photosynthesis with membranes inside the cell. Both use CO2, chlorophyll and water.

2.why: Chemoautotrophs get their energy from inorganic chemicals, not light. Photoautotrophs use light.

3.why: The light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) happen in the stroma. The light reactions happen in the thylakoids.

4.why: A granum is a stack of thylakoids.

5.why: Photosynthesis makes sugars and oxygen. CO2 is something it uses up, not makes.

6.why: Glucose is the main fuel cells break down for energy.

7.why: Ultraviolet light has short wavelengths and high energy, enough to damage DNA.

8.why: The energy of a wave is measured by its wavelength: shorter means more energy.

9.why: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths, so they carry the least energy.

10.why: The book stresses that carotenoids absorb extra energy and get rid of it as heat, protecting the plant. They also widen the colors a plant can use, so (a) counts too.

11.why: A photosystem has antenna pigments, a reaction center and a primary electron acceptor. ATP synthase is a separate protein.

12.why: The antenna complex just catches light and passes the energy along. It doesn't move electrons or pump H+.

13.why: Wavelength tells you how much energy the light carries.

14.why: CO2 has to keep coming in, because its carbon is what gets fixed into sugar. RuBP and RuBisCO are reused.

15.why: RuBP + CO<sub>2</sub> → (RuBisCO) → 3-PGA → G3P. That's fixation, then reduction.

16.why: Carbon fixation means turning inorganic CO2 into an organic compound.

17.why: RuBisCO is the enzyme that attaches CO2 to RuBP.

18.why: Plants and animals both do cellular respiration. Only plants do photosynthesis.

19.why: Bacteria in your intestines eat what you eat, so they're heterotrophs. The others all photosynthesize.

20.why: RuBisCO catalyzes the reaction between CO2 and RuBP, the fixation step.

21.why: The Calvin cycle's direct product is G3P (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate). Glucose is built from it afterwards.

22.why: The light reactions make ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle spends them to build sugars.

23.why: The light-dependent reactions make NADPH and ATP, which power the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle).

24.why: Photosynthesis uses energy to build carbohydrates. Respiration breaks them down to release energy. Each is the other in reverse.

25.why: Light hits PS II first, which excites chlorophyll a electrons. They go down the transport chain through the cytochrome complex from PS II to PS I, and the products (ATP and NADPH) power the Calvin cycle.

26.why: UV and X-rays have short wavelengths and high energy, enough to get into tissue and damage cells and DNA.

27.why: Yes. Chlorophyll absorbs red light well, so photosynthesis can still happen.

28.why: Splitting water at PS II supplies electrons, which travel down the chain to PS I.

29.why: Without enough CO<sub>2</sub>, the Calvin cycle has nothing to fix, so photosynthesis slows down or stops.

30.why: The cycle makes G3P and regenerates RuBP so it can fix more CO2.

31.why: CAM plants open their stomata at night, when it's cooler, to take in CO2, and keep them closed in the heat of the day to save water.

32.why: Lions eat herbivores, and herbivores eat plants (autotrophs). So the lion's energy traces back to photosynthesis.

33.why: Each turn fixes one carbon, and G3P has three, so it takes 3 turns to fix enough carbon to send out one G3P.

34.why: Both electron transport chains use a cytochrome complex. Chloroplasts, photosystems and thylakoids belong only to photosynthesis.

35.why: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and glucose, the very things photosynthesis makes. These shared, linked pathways point to common ancestry.

36.why: A = outer membrane, B = stroma (the fluid), C = granum (a stack), D = thylakoid, E = inner membrane.

37.why: Chloroplasts and mitochondria both have double membranes, and both electron transport chains use a cytochrome complex.

38.why: Making ATP by chemiosmosis needs a membrane to hold the H+ gradient, and the thylakoid membrane is that membrane.

39.why: The cycle spends 6 ATP and 6 NADPH to make G3P, which stores the energy, and uses more ATP to regenerate RuBP.

40.why: NADP<sup>+</sup> is given back when the Calvin cycle uses NADPH. With too little CO<sub>2</sub>, the cycle stalls, NADPH isn't used, and the plant runs out of NADP<sup>+</sup>.

41.why: Losing CO<sub>2</sub> leaves the Calvin cycle without enough carbon to fix, so it slows down or stops, even with plenty of light and water.

42.why: Plastoquinone and plastocyanin pass electrons along through redox reactions, toward photosystem I.

43.why: The light-reaction parts (photosystems I and II and NADP+ reductase) sit in the thylakoid membrane. The Calvin cycle chemicals are kept separate inside the chloroplast.

44.why: Chlorophylls barely absorb green (they reflect it). The book says β-carotene absorbs blue and green, so carotenoids would lose the least.

45.why: Antenna pigments pass light energy along until it reaches the chlorophyll a pair in the reaction center. That pair hands an excited electron to the primary electron acceptor, and the lost electron is replaced from water.
